_about.what: Data behind site-management-roadmap.html. Every ticket object has two halves: STATIC fields authored from the ticket scope files, and LIVE fields (pmTicketNumber / pmStatus / pmAssignee / pmUrl) that stay null until the tickets exist in BIS PM.
_about.authority: parent-site-management-mvp.md is the source of truth for every STATIC field. Do not invent tickets or dependencies here.
_about.axes: TWO INDEPENDENT AXES, and conflating them is the mistake the old tier system made. TIER is timing — A ships with MVP, B builds in parallel, C comes after, D is backlog. PREFIX is ownership — SM- is Site-Management-specific, S- serves the whole platform. A ticket's prefix does not determine its tier: S-01 is an S-ticket in Tier A, SM-08 is an SM-ticket in Tier D. Prefix is derived from the key in the page; it is not a stored field.
_about.structure: Graph structure comes from each ticket's dependsOn (hard prerequisites) and relatedTo (relationships that do not gate the target). edgeMeta only decorates those edges with a kind + note; an edge with no edgeMeta entry defaults to kind 'required'. Stage/layer position is computed in the page by longest-path layering, so adding a dependency re-lays-out the graph automatically.
_about.nonTicketFields: Three fields carry things the edge model cannot. `blockedByAlso` is an array of non-ticket blockers (a pending decision, a pre-build confirmation) — real gates with no card to draw an arrow from. `blocksNote` qualifies an empty Blocks list. `related` is a display-only relationship list that deliberately draws NO edge, so a ticket that blocks nothing still reads as connected to the tickets it touches.
_about.conflicts: Top-level `conflicts` records cross-ticket disagreements that are flagged and NOT fixed. Each names the tickets it sits between; the page derives a warning chip on each of those cards and lists the conflict in full in the About view. Nothing here is a decision.
_about.order: Within a stage, cards render in the order tickets appear in this array. That order is chosen to minimise connector crossings — reorder deliberately. The register groups by tier and preserves the same order inside each group.

_refresh.summary: Claude refreshes this file; the browser never calls BIS PM. A page opened from file:// cannot fetch a sibling JSON, so the HTML carries an inline mirror of this file.
steps: 2. For every ticket where pmTicketNumber is NOT null, call mcp__pmMCP__getTicketDetails with that number.
3. Write the result into that ticket's LIVE fields: pmStatus (the PM status string), pmAssignee (display name or null), pmUrl (the BIS PM ticket URL). Leave every STATIC field untouched.
4. For tickets that have since been created in BIS PM, set pmTicketNumber first (find it with mcp__pmMCP__getTicketList or getTicketsByGroup), then do step 3. pmUrl is what makes a card clickable.
5. Set meta.lastRefreshed to an ISO-8601 timestamp. The page renders it in the masthead; null renders as 'never'.

7. CRITICAL — also rewrite the inline mirror inside site-management-roadmap.html, between the ROADMAP-DATA:BEGIN and ROADMAP-DATA:END comment markers. The two must stay byte-identical, or a double-clicked page will show stale data. The page footer reports which source it actually used.
notes: No tickets exist in BIS PM yet, so every LIVE field starts null and every card shows the muted '#—' placeholder chip. This page is published to a public repo, so live BIS PM URLs are a separate decision — do not fill these in without being asked.
S-03, SM-06 and SM-07 are flagged 'Create ticket now' in the scope files — they are the likely first three to get real numbers.
Nothing in the HTML fetches anything at runtime except Google Fonts. There is no build step.

meta.title: Site Management — build order and dependencies
meta.standfirst: Fourteen tickets on two independent axes. Tier is timing; the SM- / S- prefix is ownership. This is the dependency spine: what has to land first, what builds alongside it, and what explicitly does not gate the MVP.

A.note: Blocks release. The MVP does not ship until every one of these lands.

B.note: Does not block the MVP, and is active now.

SM.name: Site Management

conflicts.title: Two mechanisms claim the competency gate
conflicts.what: The object model routes LMS → Attendance (S-04) for a competency check at sign-in. SM-06 gates the same need on Site Access instead.
conflicts.state: Two mechanisms, one need, and no decision on which owns it. Resolve before either ticket is estimated — whichever loses is carrying scope it should not have.

conflicts.title: Meetings' signing route assumes scope Attendance does not claim
conflicts.what: The stated route is that Meetings collects signatures through Attendance rather than building its own capture. But a meeting is explicitly not a form, and S-04's mechanism is form-bound — the narrowed S-04 no longer delivers attendance outside a form.
conflicts.state: Either S-04 widens to support signing detached from a form submission — scope it does not currently claim — or "through Attendance" means reusing a shared signature component rather than S-04's actual mechanism. Undecided. Read side by side, the two ticket files currently contradict each other.

edgeMeta.note: A ritual attaches to a site and reads its operating calendar.
"A named set of sites" has no meaning until the Site object exists.
A scannable Site cannot exist before the Site object does — SM-01 is what supplies the alternative to "must be an owned asset".
SM-01's conversion feature creates Sites flat; sub-site structure is deferred here on purpose.
The mobile surfaces render Site state, so there is nothing to render until the Site object exists.
Nothing else in the list functions without the Site object.
Crew supplies the name list that pre-populates the attendance field.
The "My Crew" view in the supervisor surface.
The agreed minimum scope populates a meeting's people list by reusing the crew import, so Meetings cannot be built before Crew exists.
View-without-edit and site membership both hang off Crew.
Crew-as-subject grants only. Individual-subject grants are NOT blocked by Crew — the earlier framing that S-02 is wholly downstream of Crew was too strong.
Blocks the parent's "surfacing what's outstanding" scope.
The SM slice must ship for SM to push — the comparison has to know which forms count toward which site.

Named in the parent's Blocked by line.

tickets.title: Site object
tickets.summary: The place work happens — it holds what's owed and the operating calendar, and shows current vs N outstanding. Built as a new object alongside Site Access, which stays exactly as it is for MVP. The operating calendar is which days this site works, inherited from a company default and overridden per site.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking. Nothing else in this list functions without it.
tickets.boundary: Assets keeps things — vehicles, equipment, properties. Site keeps place and work context.
tickets.evidence: 4 clients tried Assets as an organisational construct and abandoned it. Product leadership's decisive point: an asset can only have one assigned person, and an asset-used-as-a-site can't tell who's on it or what's owed.

tickets.title: Forms report to the right site
tickets.summary: Count a form toward the site the work was for — not the worker's home location. A submission can declare the work context it reports against — business unit, job, customer site, crew — independent of where the submitter is based or where they physically were. The data often already exists on the submission; the gap is that the reporting layer can't query it. Not a new hierarchy: an attribute clients already fill in that the system currently drops.
tickets.slice: Only the read path: SM can group and count forms by the site the work was for, so the comparison knows which forms count toward which site.

related.note: Probably the same underlying issue: the missing form-to-job join key is what blocks the Job anchor.
The same reporting subsystem from a different direction — one form pointing at the right site, versus one metric spanning several forms.

tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking — this slice must ship for SM to push. Moved into Tier A on 2026-08-27: it was always MVP-blocking and only sat in the old "Tier B" because that system conflated ownership with timing. The full initiative (reporting filtering, hierarchy separation, retrofitting existing submissions) is post-SM and not blocking.
tickets.boundary: Likely the first slice of something larger. Getting a form to report against the work context it was for — rather than the submitter's home location — is the same underlying problem as tying reports generally to the right place. That larger initiative isn't scoped and isn't this ticket. What Site Management needs is only the read path: SM can group and count forms by the site the work was for. The reporting-layer half, where the client-visible payoff lands, ships on its own timeline.
openQuestions: Pre-build schema check — the single biggest sizing question. Does the form-submission header carry its own location column, or is location always resolved through the user record? If it already has one, this ticket shrinks substantially. About 10 minutes for a dev, and nothing should be estimated before it is answered.

Is every client's work-context field the same field? One client carries a business unit, another links to a job, a third needs a customer site that doesn't exist as an object. This may be one configurable attribute or three problems wearing the same coat.

Can the slice ship on derived context alone, or does it need explicit selection too? Derived context covers the happy path with zero configuration, but a form completed outside any ritual — done unprompted, or filled in late — would carry no site and count toward nothing. That makes N outstanding wrong in the direction that erodes trust fastest: the work was done and the system still says it's missing.
Two of the six client attributions are verified directly against source; the other four come from cross-interview synthesis and haven't been checked against the per-source evidence banks.
tickets.evidence: Six clients across two corpora describe the same failure. Likely the same underlying issue as the form-to-job join key that blocks the Job anchor — 4 of 15, the largest anchor group, and probably the single biggest coverage lever in the backlog.

tickets.title: Crew object
tickets.summary: Who's answerable for a site, as distinct from who did the work — membership changes daily, and a site takes crews and/or individually added people. Built as a system-wide grouping tool rather than an SM-only feature, so it also serves evaluator lists and delegation fallback. Permissions stay deliberately coarse: none / read-only / full edit.
tickets.boundary: Not work dispatch, not a static org chart. View-without-edit only for MVP.
openQuestions: Is crew membership dated, or current-state only? Dated is more expensive, but current-state-only means historical records silently misreport who was there — and this is a record layer.

Does universal assignability change this ticket's bucket? Crew is SM-prefixed because SM drives it and SM's team builds it. If it ships as a system-wide assignment target it behaves like an S-ticket — the build is the same either way, the question is who owns it after MVP.
tickets.evidence: 7 of 15 clients have no crew object and bend Location into one. Named Crew, not Group — decided, because Group collides with the existing Permission Group / Company Group feature in BIS Admin.

tickets.title: Ritual object
tickets.summary: A named bundle of things that belong together — forms and tasks for MVP — defined once centrally and reused across sites. Two layers: the ritual is what's in the bundle; the attachment is which site does it and on what cadence. Cadence lives on the attachment, so the same ritual runs daily at one site and weekly at another.

related.note: Overlapping but distinct axes — a ritual bundles what a site owes, a category bundles what a metric spans. Decide which layer owns grouping before building both.

tickets.boundary: Sites only for v1 — not crews, not assets. Only recurring rituals can be outstanding; triggered ones like Incident have no cadence and never appear in the site state view.
openQuestions: Cadence granularity is not a push trigger. The system can know a second FLHA is owed at shift change without notifying anyone at 2pm — without this line someone builds 8am notifications and reintroduces the time-based push a client already reverted from.
Name unresolved. Product leadership dislikes the term ritual but offered no alternative — task and job are taken, requirement implies pre-existing. The objection was registered as non-blocking.
One client's no-rhythm case (1–10 per shift, no predictable pattern) may not be expressible as a cadence at all. Decide explicitly rather than forcing a rule that fits badly.

Two pre-build schema checks, about 25 minutes total: what columns the existing form-frequency settings table carries, and whether any working-days / operating-calendar table exists anywhere. Neither should be estimated around until answered.
scope: Cadence vocabulary: fixed interval, working-days-only, use-triggered, metered, sub-day / shift-based
Freeform scheduling with exceptions
A starter ritual library so day one isn't blank
Trigger: a ritual assigns once a person is confirmed on site — not the clock, not person scan-in
tickets.evidence: Cadence is not a recurrence rule. A daily check at a site that works 27 days in a 31-day month would count 31 days owed against 27 worked — 4 phantom misses per site, every month. The client was plain that the engine gets discarded if it does that.

tickets.title: Mobile
tickets.summary: Supervisor and worker surfaces — SM's mobile half as one ticket, one platform, one team, carrying the offline and device-profile decisions with it. The shape is settled: a layer that annotates surfaces people already use rather than becoming its own area, phone-primary and often shared. Worker-side is pull, never push, with dual visibility so a site-assigned item also appears in the normal assigned-forms list.

related.note: Signer identity on shared devices — the existing remote/deferred signing path may already answer it.

blockedByAlso: The parent's comparison logic — mobile consumes computed state, it does not compute it.
The offline decision (section 3) — sync or degrade. This is the blocking decision, and it is not made.
tickets.mvpNote: MVP-blocking — named in the parent's Blocked by line. Only its supervisor scope (section A) waits on S-02, and only for which sites a supervisor sees.
tickets.boundary: Not work dispatch. No time-of-day push, never delivered as assignments, and it must tolerate late and backdated submissions.
openQuestions: Offline behaviour undecided. The comparison is server-side — either the obligation set syncs to the device or the mobile surface degrades to something that works offline. One client runs 50–80% no-signal sites; at another, operators go days without connectivity.

Shared devices mean per-person signatures can't rely on who's logged in — needs a lightweight identify-the-signer step, not a full logout/login. Check the existing remote-signing path first; the question may go away rather than need solving.

Is the worker surface (section B) actually MVP-blocking? Section A has strong evidence and supervisors are the reliable mobile users. Section B's reach is genuinely questionable — at one client field workers never return to the app after orientation, at another ~75% of work zones are no-device, and at a third 15 of 49 projects refuse the app. Real demand, limited reach.
Which team and repo owns this? The mobile app is a different codebase from the backend — this may need splitting by repo even though it is one product surface.
scope: A. Supervisor site/crew overview + light admin actions
B. Worker "what's here" surface — context and navigation, not a task list
C. Site identification — scan, geolocation, or a planned site list (nice to have)
D. Web ↔ mobile parity — decide deliberately what is app-only, web-only, or both
tickets.evidence: One client's #1 ask is explicitly mobile. A mobile-first safety administrator at another client has to leave the app for mobile web today. At a third, bulk-add attendees is web-only — the highest-volume, most time-critical task sits on the platform the foreman isn't holding.

tickets.title: Site Management MVP
tickets.summary: The parent ticket. It carries the full MVP scope and links each child, so QA and reviewers can see the whole project in one view. Done, in client terms: a corporate safety lead at a 52-branch client opens Site Management, sees every branch reading current or N outstanding, clicks into one branch and sees what it owed this month against what was done — and builds nothing to get there.
tickets.blocksNote: It is the end of the graph — everything else flows into it.
tickets.mvpNote: This is the MVP. It ships when its five blockers ship.
tickets.boundary: A record and omission layer, not a work dispatch tool. Don't build a place to work; build a place that proves work happened and says what's missing.
scope: Sites index — current / N outstanding per site. MVP renders Sites only
Single-site view — owed vs done this period
Day-one empty state — what a client sees with zero configuration
Surfacing what's outstanding
Real-time event view
Notification triggers
Calendar view + past-day lookup — low priority
Ad-hoc assignment — low priority
tickets.evidence: The risk that outranks every ticket is configuration burden. A safety lead with 52 branches was handed a working config path to her own #1 pain and never did it — it was simply too much. If the best-case user won't configure it, nobody will, so every decision is measured against what a client gets on day one with zero configuration.

tickets.title: Scoped permissions
tickets.summary: Separate view from edit; grant across a named set of sites. Two open interaction models — a share sheet (subject → access level) vs. named custom roles with a per-object grid. Both evidenced; present both, don't pick one before the room does. Every grant has two halves, a subject (a crew or an individual) and a scope (a named set of sites), and grants are additive only — a grant can give access, never remove it.
tickets.slice: SM-scoped custom permissions built into the new module out of the box — it helps SM-04's supervisor view and SM-02's view-without-edit grant.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier B — parallel build, active now, and it does not block the MVP. What is open is not whether it ships but which interaction model it ships as. Product leadership's read: system-wide custom roles are a large build, but building it out of the box inside a new module is acceptable.
tickets.boundary: Sites are the only scope type for now. The system-wide custom-permissions overhaul this ticket splits off from is a separate initiative and is not in scope here.
openQuestions: Option A or Option B? Share sheet or custom roles — the room decides, not this document. Option A is cheaper and needs zero configuration to reach "can view"; Option B is more capable at the cost of an admin building roles before anyone benefits. No meeting on record has picked one.

Validate the ask first — sometimes what a client calls a permissions problem is really a reporting problem. Before any of the six clients is counted as a permissions requirement, confirm the underlying need is access and not visibility. That costs one question per client and could shrink the ticket materially.
How rich is "richer"? A view/edit split per object type, per screen, per field? Undecided, and it is the main sizing lever — effectively the same question as Option A or B.
Is the additive union always safe? Additive-only avoids a precedence engine, but nobody has checked for a case where the union over-grants in a way a client would object to.
At one client the only available workaround breaks their payroll-system integration.
No technical investigation stands behind this ticket. The technical-findings work covers S-01, S-04 and SM-03; it does not cover permissions. Treat the sizing as unevidenced.
tickets.evidence: 6 clients, ranked #1 by two. One client's record-validator is forced into full admin because there is nothing in between learner and admin — she is now doing things she should not be doing. Another has no supervisor role in the organisation at all, which is why individual subjects cannot be optional.

tickets.title: Attendance with individual signatures
tickets.summary: Individual signatures, crew pre-populated. ⚠ Approach contested. Two positions are on record — pre-populate the existing attendance form field as a quick win, versus building phase 1 of the standalone attendance tool instead rather than extending a field the platform intends to phase out. This ticket documents the narrower option; it is not a decision.
tickets.slice: Crew pre-population on the attendance field, so ritual fulfilment is trustworthy — toolbox talks are the most common ritual in the corpus.
tickets.blocksNote: Nothing waits on it. SM-07 used to, and no longer does — which is a problem rather than a simplification. See the flagged conflict.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier B — parallel build, active now. Not release-blocking: today's bulk-attest already produces a signal the comparison can match against, so individual signing makes the record correct rather than possible.
tickets.boundary: Attendance capture only. The meeting / toolbox-talk content object is split out as SM-07. A universal cross-system signing tool stays the long-term goal, not the MVP.
openQuestions: The approach itself is contested and goes to the presentation meeting. A later session decided to build a standalone phase-1 attendance tool with an explicit no-linking rule between the two, and redefined the MVP as a supervisor checklist and nothing more. This ticket's current content reflects the earlier direction and needs a rewrite pass before it is presented as current.

How is presence actually established? Crew says who is assigned, not who turned up. Four candidate modes — supervisor checklist, self sign-in, QR scan, geotag — and they are not equally good. Treat them as one presence record with four sources, and put a source value on the record from day one.

Recommend against geofencing for MVP: it asserts presence with no human action, needs an always-on permission that app-hostile crews will not grant, raises consultation and privacy questions, and fails for accuracy exactly where it is needed. The salvageable version is geo as corroboration — stamp the location when someone taps "I'm here".
Is the per-signature timestamp persisted, or render-time only? Decides whether one client's regulator finding is a toggle or a schema change. About 10 minutes for a dev.
Is the attendee user-id nullable — are free-text/guest attendees allowed? If guests exist, "everyone signs beside their own name" has an unresolvable subset. This is the ticket's real technical risk.

Why isn't the existing per-person signing reaching clients? Not a build question — discoverability, defaults, scale, or a mobile gap. If a shipped capability isn't being adopted, shipping more configurable capability doesn't fix it, and this initiative is about to ship a lot of it.

QR scan pulls Site Access into scope, and the likely real blocker there is commercial rather than technical: Site Access is a toggled, licensed service. If SM presence must work for every client, that constraint decides it.
tickets.evidence: One client rejects bulk-attest outright for legal reasons. Another client's loudest single ask is to stop making foremen retype 20–30 names, and that same client has no timestamps on FLHA entries — the safety regulator flagged it after an accident. Unlocks the most common ritual in the corpus: 11 of 15 run toolbox talks.

tickets.title: Job
tickets.summary: An engagement with an address and a lifespan — distinct from a Site, doesn't require one. Serves the largest single compliance anchor in the corpus: 4 of 15 clients. A Job has its own address, its own lifespan (start, expected end, actual close), and may optionally attach to a Site where a client's reality nests that way — but it never needs one.

related.note: The ownership-direction question: does a Crew own many Jobs, or a Job own a Crew? Only one client's evidence, and it reads as crew-owns-jobs.
Probably the same anchor S-01's coverage argument names — the missing form-to-job join key is what leaves this group unserved.
Two of S-03's three originally cited clients moved here on re-verification: their root problem was a missing container, not un-groupable forms.

tickets.blocksNote: Nothing waits on it — including the MVP's web interface. The Sites index will need a second row-shape once Job lands, but that is later work, not a gate.
tickets.maturity: Newer and less validated than the rest of the initiative — same-day new as of 2026-08-27. It has not been through the technical-findings process the older tickets had, and its open questions are more genuinely open than most. Read the confidence here as lower across the board.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier B — parallel build, active now, and it blocks nothing. Whether it stays in B or moves to A once a second data point confirms the pattern generalises is itself an open question.
tickets.boundary: Not a rename of Site. Site answers "what does this place owe"; Job answers "is this engagement done". Presence and sign-in stay Site's territory for MVP — a Job's address is reporting-grade, not a boundary to check in against. No Jobs nesting inside Jobs, and no automatic close.
openQuestions: Does Job attach to Crew, or Crew to Job? One client's evidence reads as crew-owns-many-jobs — one gang holding around ten open jobs, hopping between them because work stops pending permits, with nothing marking which job is tonight's. Untested against a second client.
Does a Job have its own operating calendar, inherit one from an attached Site, or need none at all?
Is a multi-job day one page, or one page per job? Unsettled between two participants on the research call itself — a real open UX question, not yet a decision.
Does this belong in Tier B permanently, or move to Tier A once a second data point confirms the pattern generalises?
scope: Address — light and reporting-grade, not the presence-capable address a Site carries
Start date, optional expected end, and an actual close a person confirms — never an automatic close on the expected-end date
Standalone by default — a Job may optionally attach to a Site, and never needs one. This is the config-burden answer for Job: no scaffolding required to create one
The same attachment contract as Site — a Job holds Rituals, Attendance and Meetings, and feeds the owed-vs-done comparison exactly as a Site does
tickets.evidence: Four of 15 clients' compliance unit is an engagement, not a place — the largest single anchor in the corpus, bigger than place (3) or asset (2) individually, and today none of them have a container for it. One client is the cleanest case: the unit is the job — the residence plus the event plus the document set — and every disqualifier for the other two objects is explicit in one sentence, because the address is one-shot and the crews dissolve nightly. At another, the only link between a form and a job is a job number typed into the form's content, which is the structural defect that produces the retrieval pain.

tickets.title: Form grouping / category layer
tickets.summary: A category above the form so one metric can span several. ⚠ Evidence narrowed — 2 of its 3 original clients moved to SM-09. A grouping layer over existing forms, not a change to forms themselves.
tickets.slice: Site-level status lines that span several forms — the multi-branch client's branch scorecard and per-branch rollup.

related.note: Where the evidence went: two of the three originally cited clients were re-verified as needing the Job object, because their root problem was a missing container rather than un-groupable forms.
Overlapping but distinct axes — a ritual bundles what a site owes, a category bundles what a metric spans.
The same reporting subsystem from a different direction, and the ticket that relativises this one's coverage claim.

tickets.blocksNote: Nothing in the MVP — decided Aug 24. SM-03's ritual bundle already groups what a site owes.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after MVP, scheduled but not urgent. Created now anyway, because it is the upsell and taking it to product was committed on a client call.
openQuestions: Evidence under revision. Two previously cited clients have been re-verified as needing the Job object (SM-09) instead. Only the branch-scorecard case and the discipline-grouping example remain valid support. The coverage-lever claim and the "three or four more clients" upsell figure both need updating — do not present the current evidence list as current until that pass happens.

Rituals (SM-03) may be able to serve this, or it may need its own axis. Worth deciding rather than building both — the cheapest test is to express the branch scorecard in each model and see which one strains.

What does outstanding mean for a category of mixed cadences? Is the category outstanding if any member form is, all of them, or weighted? No client has been asked, and it decides whether the branch scorecard is a number anyone trusts.
Can a form live in more than one category? Exclusive is simpler and probably wrong. Decide before the data model is fixed.
No sizing evidence exists. The "two more months" figure in the upsell framing is a talking point, not an estimate — do not let it harden into a commitment.
Who owns this after MVP? It is an S-ticket: it serves the whole platform, and reporting is not the Site Management team's module. Site Management is the reason it gets prioritised, not its home.
tickets.evidence: A 52-branch client runs 30+ forms at mixed cadences and every metric they want spans several. Already committed on a client call to take to product — which is why the ticket gets created now even though it is not in the MVP.

tickets.title: Object-scan to open the right form
tickets.summary: Scan an asset and its form, task or folder opens immediately — context supplied, no list to hunt through. Extends what already works; the unblock is removing the requirement that the scanned thing be an owned asset, which is the restriction that lost one client's business.

related.note: When a scanned Site owes a bundle, the ritual is what the scan should resolve to.
The attendance field's existing QR-code option may be this same mechanism approached from the other end. Check it before building a second one.

blockedByAlso: The offline decision in SM-04 section 3.
A pre-build confirmation — scope is not honestly estimable until someone says where the owned-asset requirement is actually enforced.
tickets.blocksNote: Nothing critical. SM-04 section 4C names scan as one of its site-identification mechanisms — without SM-05 that degrades to its other mechanisms rather than failing, which is why 4C is a nice-to-have and this is Tier C.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after MVP, scheduled but not urgent. It makes the worker-facing entry point better; nothing critical waits on it.
openQuestions: Where is the owned-asset requirement enforced? Nothing here is honestly estimable until that is answered — it is the cheapest unblocking action on the ticket.
tickets.evidence: Works today and is well liked. Clients describe the pattern as walking past a thing, scanning it, filling in the form and moving on. Unlocks the worker-facing entry point that demonstrably works, as opposed to time-based push, which one client already reverted.

tickets.title: Multi-topic competency gate on Site Access
tickets.summary: Check more than one competency before granting site entry. ⚠ Conflicts with S-04 on mechanism. References existing LMS state rather than building new data. Runs standalone; SM consumes the result, which turns Site Access from an in/out tracker into SM's competency signal.

related.note: Via the eventual Site Access replacement path, not via MVP scope — SM-01 leaves Site Access untouched for MVP, and this is the ticket that changes it.

tickets.blocksNote: Nothing on the MVP critical path. The parent's interface can consume the competency signal if it exists, and simply doesn't show it if it doesn't.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after MVP. Runs standalone, and deliberately sits outside the MVP.
tickets.boundary: Build the check as a service — given a person and a set of competency topics, is each one valid and if not why not — callable from anywhere, not as logic embedded in the Site Access entry screen. That costs nothing now and is the difference between re-pointing and rewriting when Site Access is eventually replaced.
openQuestions: Which mechanism owns the competency gate — this ticket's Site Access route, or the LMS-to-Attendance route in S-04? Unresolved, and it must be settled before either ticket is estimated.
Site-entry vs work-authorisation are being conflated — different features, different data requirements. Resolve first.

Small build, real data-fitness risk. Two independent clients say the underlying training data isn't fit to gate on as-is: at one, expiry dates are wrong in both directions; at the other, only the trained third of competency is modelled at all. Worth a short spike before treating this as a quick win.

State the evidence base honestly: one client and one scenario. No other client in the 15 raised multi-topic gating, and only one or two clients use Site Access at all. That is not a reason to drop it — the scenario is sharp and the ask was unprompted — but it is a reason not to size it as if it had corpus-wide backing.
Nobody who owns the Site Access replacement has signed off on the extend-vs-replace reasoning, and that replacement has no date, no scope and no owner recorded.
tickets.evidence: One client's #1 ask, raised unprompted. An electrical contractor with a valid induction but an expired licence walks straight through the gate.

tickets.title: Meetings
tickets.summary: The object behind a daily safety meeting or toolbox talk, client-labelled. Trigger and object model decided; signing route open. Clients call it different things — safety meetings, daily safety meetings, toolbox talks — so the object carries a client-set custom name rather than one the product picks. Split out of S-04 because product leadership ruled out building the attendance tool and this at the same time.

related.note: A meeting may be a ritual, or may sit inside one — worth settling before build.
The calendar view lands on the mobile surface.
No longer a blocker, and that is the problem — see the flagged conflict on signing.

tickets.mvpNote: Tier C — after MVP. Corrected from a brief placement in Tier D during the tier migration, which undersold it: a ticket actively being sized is not a shelved one. C is the honest floor, and an effort estimate is the deciding input for whether it moves up.
tickets.boundary: A meeting is deliberately not a form. The minimal version is a title, an upload of what is being talked about, and a signature — plus reporting on who attended which one.
openQuestions: The signing route is open. Route A builds self-contained signing inside Meetings — ships independently, at the cost of a third signing implementation in the platform. Route B waits for a broader standalone attendance/signing tool, which has no ticket. A route has been named, but it points at S-04, whose current scope cannot deliver it.

Can the existing per-attendee signing path be invoked without a form submission? Per-attendee signing already exists in code, but it is bound to the form attendance field and assumes a submission exists to hang off. This single question decides whether Route A is a modest reuse or a genuine build, and it is the cheapest unblocking action on the ticket.
Tier coupling. If this joins the MVP, whatever it depends on for signing must join the MVP with it. A Tier C ticket must not quietly pull an unticketed, unestimated tool into the release.

The name has drifted across three revisions before landing on Meetings, and some upstream files still carry the older combined label. Flagged for whoever owns them; the object itself should carry a client-set custom name rather than any of the three.
tickets.evidence: Product leadership wants it and rates it highly — daily safety meetings happen everywhere and there's no good way to handle it. The signing half is easy; the content half is the gap. Scoping a meeting to a crew is also what fixes one client's chase-everyone problem: today toolbox talks go out company-wide and someone then checks who hasn't signed, one person at a time.

tickets.title: Sub-site work sections
tickets.summary: Multiple work areas or job numbers beneath one physical site. Likely mobile and transient rather than fixed structure — and possibly expressible as Crews rather than as sub-sites, which is worth testing before building a new hierarchy level.

related.note: Test whether Crew already expresses this before adding a hierarchy level.
Shares two of this ticket's three clients, and may be the better answer to the one-crew-six-job-numbers case.

tickets.blocksNote: Nothing in the initiative waits on this.
tickets.mvpNote: Tier D — backlog, not scheduled. Revisit post-MVP.
openQuestions: A migration question worth answering before clients import at scale. SM-01's conversion feature creates Sites flat. If a client converts 200 Locations into flat Sites now and sub-sites arrive later, do those Sites need restructuring — and is that a manual re-do or a supported migration? Cheaper to answer before people import than after.
Sub-sites or crews? The one-neighbourhood-many-crews case may be a Crew problem, not a hierarchy problem. Test before building.

Does the deferral rationale still hold when you read this? It rests on the claim that the clients who need it aren't served by the MVP anyway — which is a statement about a moment. Re-check it against S-01's status rather than assuming.

What does a sub-unit carry? Can a Ritual attach to a work section, or only to a Site? Can a Crew be assigned to a section rather than the whole site? Both change the size considerably, and neither has been asked.
tickets.evidence: One client runs 6 job numbers on one physical site with one crew, already worked around via multi-asset attachment. At another, a single neighbourhood holds three concrete crews, two paving crews and an underground crew, each with its own FLHA.
